title: Lisnagaver & Rasharkin
standfirst: Nineteenth-century records document several Glasgow households around Lisnagaver, Gortahar and Kilrea. Their shared older parentage, and any route back to Larne or Inishrush, remain open.
question: Can the documented Lisnagaver, Gortahar and Kilrea households be joined by a record that names their older parents, rather than by shared surname, locality, or DNA alone?
answer: Alexander’s probable father is John Glasgow, farmer, named in John-867’s 1846 marriage: Nancy’s probate citation and independently documented Glasgow birth surnames favour a common paternal sibling group. No record names Alexander’s own father directly. The Thomas–Daniel family is independently proved but is not joined to Alexander by a parent statement. The Desertoghill and Larne identities remain separate hypotheses.

chapters.title: A local network before the later families
body: The study keeps nearby Inishrush and Bann Valley material as comparison evidence, not as an inherited pedigree. Adam and John at Inishrush may be related, but no inspected record calls them brothers or names a shared parent.
The 1831 household return records separate Adam and John Glasgow households in Inishrush; it does not list household members by name.

chapters.title: Alexander and Mary’s documented family
body: Baptisms, the complete 1851 household and later marriages document Alexander Glasgow and Mary McCaughan and six children. Their descendant evidence places a tested line in R-FT20271.

John Glasgow, farmer, is Alexander’s probable father through Nancy’s reconstructed sibling group. Her newly inspected 1891 death notice gives about 75, conflicting with the age in her will; it confirms her Plattsburgh death and funeral but names no parents. The Glenleslie Nancy who died in 1847 is a different woman. Mary McCaughan’s parents remain unresolved.

chapters.title: John and Margaret at Lisnagaver
body: The 1846 marriage, 1851 household and family memorial establish John Glasgow, Margaret Garvin, their children and John’s brother Samuel.

John’s original 1846 marriage names his father John Glasgow, farmer. The record-defined father is represented by Glasgow-4090; identifying him with the 1796 Desertoghill occupier or Glenleslie John is a separate unproved step.

chapters.title: Thomas and Daniel are brothers
body: Daniel’s will calls Thomas his late brother and Daniel Neely Glasgow his nephew. Daniel Neely’s marriage names Thomas as father.
That evidence proves the brotherhood and nephew relationship, but does not name Thomas and Daniel’s parents or prove Alexander was their brother.

Two Belfast death notices identify [Daniel Glasgow](/people/glasgow-3896.html) at Church Street, Kilrea, on 16 October 1871. They give age 73; his civil registration gives 75. These repeated notices corroborate the death date and address but leave a two-year birth-age discrepancy. They do not identify the brothers’ parents or connect them to Alexander’s family.

chapters.title: Later documented continuations
body: Daniel Neely Glasgow and Mary Jane Boyd’s marriage and original birth returns document daughters Sarah Taylor and Elizabeth Boyd. Mary Ann Glasgow’s marriage names Alexander as her father and later records continue the Elder household.
These continuations do not settle the older Glasgow-parentage question.

chapters.title: Lisnagaver newspaper context
body: The Belfast News-Letter of 5 June 1829 lists No. 2324, Alex. Glasgow, Lisnagaver, among applications to register freeholds under 10 Geo IV c. 8; the description gives lands in Kilconway barony and Lisnagaver townland. This is an application only: no age, kinship, admission or successful registration is stated.

The original page is now inspected, resolving the earlier access gap. [Alexander Glasgow-951](/people/glasgow-951.html) and [older Alexander Glasgow-3904](/people/glasgow-3904.html) remain compatible applicant candidates. The conflicting age estimates remain open; no parentage confidence changes.

A 7 January 1861 report names Robt. Glasgow as a Lisnagaver neighbour who warned James M’Caughern before a house collapse and narrowly escaped. [Robert Glasgow-938](/people/glasgow-938.html) and [Robert Glasgow-3449](/people/glasgow-3449.html) remain compatible candidates. No age, kinship or property bridge is stated.

clusters.title: Alexander Glasgow and Mary McCaughan
clusters.summary: Baptisms, the complete 1851 household and later marriages document the couple and six children. A tested descendant is in R-FT20271.
clusters.boundary: Alexander’s parents, the named ancestor shared with James J, and his exact relationship to Thomas and Daniel remain unresolved. The 1888 death remains probable, with age and informant identity unresolved.

clusters.title: John Glasgow and Margaret Garvin
clusters.summary: The 1846 marriage, 1851 household and family memorial establish the couple, their children and John’s brother Samuel.
clusters.boundary: The older father John is named but not securely identified with an existing profile.

clusters.title: Thomas and Daniel Glasgow
clusters.summary: Daniel’s will calls Thomas his late brother and Daniel Neely Glasgow his nephew; the nephew’s marriage names Thomas as father.
clusters.boundary: The records do not name the brothers’ parents or prove Alexander was their brother.

clusters.title: Daniel Neely Glasgow and Mary Jane Boyd
clusters.summary: The marriage and original birth returns document the couple and daughters Sarah Taylor and Elizabeth Boyd Glasgow.
clusters.boundary: Their later migration evidence does not resolve the older Glasgow parentage question.

clusters.title: Mary Ann Glasgow and Robert Elder
clusters.summary: Mary’s marriage names Alexander Glasgow as her father and later Gortahar records continue the Elder household.
clusters.boundary: Only catalogue people with public dossiers are linked here; unresolved later children remain research subjects.

clusters.title: Inishrush collateral leads
clusters.summary: Family-register, census, tithe and marriage clues identify Adam and John as meaningful comparison leads beside, not within, the later Lisnagaver households.
clusters.boundary: No document proves a bridge to Lisnagaver or Bann Valley families; Adam and John may be brothers, cousins or unrelated namesakes.

proved: Daniel and Thomas are brothers; Daniel Neely is Thomas’s son and Daniel’s nephew.
Alexander and Mary’s household, John and Margaret’s household, and Mary Ann’s father statement are documented.
supported: Nancy’s citation and independent surname records favour Alexander and John sharing a Glasgow father; John farmer is the probable father, without a direct statement for Alexander.
hypothesis: Adam and John of Inishrush may be brothers or cousins.
The Gortereghy, Drumadarragh and Finvoy McCaughan networks are candidate routes to Mary’s parentage.
unresolved: Alexander’s mother and a proved parentage bridge to Thomas and Daniel are missing; the probable John father is not automatically the Desertoghill man.
No record proves a Lisnagaver descent from Inishrush, Larne or another Irish cluster.

gaps.title: Test the probable John father independently
gaps.why: An original parent statement in Nancy’s reconstructed sibling group could strengthen or redirect the father inference without relying entirely on her probate petition.
gaps.where: Mary Thomson–Sneddon’s Old Monkland family, Ann McClelland’s own death, Nancy’s 1894 appraisal and Irish family records

gaps.title: Inspect Mary McCaughan’s original marriage or baptism evidence
gaps.why: It could identify her parents among competing local McCaughan-variant families.
gaps.where: First Kilraughts register; Gortereghy, Drumadarragh and Finvoy records

gaps.title: Obtain Daniel’s will and associated estate records
gaps.why: The will already proves the sibling network; fuller files may name the older generation or property succession.
gaps.where: Kilrea and Killoquin probate and estate records

gaps.title: Test John’s older father identity
gaps.why: A parent, residence or occupation statement could distinguish the named father from existing same-name profiles.
gaps.where: Lisnagaver leases, memorial and church records

gaps.title: Resolve the Inishrush household relationships
gaps.why: Church, lease and succession records could distinguish Adam–John brotherhood from cousin or namesake alternatives.

gaps.title: Identify a documented male-line comparator
gaps.why: A Big Y-700 result from a documented Larne/Kilwaughter or John-867 line could refine the paternal comparison without naming an ancestor by itself.
gaps.where: Glasgow DNA project and documented descent audit

sources_note: Original 1846 Irish marriage, Nancy’s will and probate citation, the newly inspected 1891 newspaper death notice, and Irish census and family records underpin the conclusions. The linked people pages distinguish records from identity hypotheses and record the bounded searches completed on 29 September 2026. The 1871 Belfast death notices repeat one account; their age of 73 is retained alongside the civil-register age of 75.
